https://nineoclock.ro/mariana-kuhnel-fma.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount ASF President Alexandru Petrescu Holds Talks with FMA Board Member Mariana Kühnel in Bucharest Romanian-Austrian cooperation in the financial sector is being strengthened through closer dialogue between the supervisory authorities of the two countries. Mariana Kühnel, a member of the Executive Board of the Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA), paid a working visit to Bucharest, where she held meetings with representatives of Romania’s key financial institutions. The agenda included meetings with Alexandru Petrescu, President of the Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF), Presidential Adviser Radu Burnete, and a Vice President of the National Bank of Romania (BNR). The discussions focused on the importance of close European cooperation and regular exchanges of information and expertise on financial market developments and supervision. The programme also included discussions with senior representatives of major Austrian companies listed on the stock exchange and active in Romania, highlighting the significant economic ties between the two countries. ASF President Alexandru Petrescu outlined the main topics discussed during his meeting with the FMA delegation in a post on his Facebook page: “Today, at the Authority’s headquarters, together with ASF First Vice President Gabriel-Ioan Avrămescu and Vice President of the Insurance-Reinsurance Sector Sorin Mititelu, I welcomed the delegation of the Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA), which included Mariana Kühnel, Executive Director of the FMA, and Martina Andexlinger, Director of the Insurance Companies and Pension Funds Supervision Department. The meeting provided an opportunity for an in-depth exchange of views on the main developments and challenges in financial regulation and supervision at European level. Discussions focused on several strategic issues of common interest: ▶️ the status of implementation of the Insurance Recovery and Resolution Directive (IRRD) and the main challenges associated with its application; ▶️ developments concerning the Markets Integration and Supervision Package (MISP), including from the perspective of strengthening European capital markets and making the supervisory framework more efficient; ▶️ the experience of the two authorities and the challenges encountered in the field of crypto-assets, in the context of the evolving European regulatory and supervisory framework. I believe that direct dialogue between the competent national authorities is essential for strengthening the European Single Market and for underpinning our contributions to discussions within EIOPA and ESMA. Such meetings allow us to better understand common challenges, share experiences and best practices, and identify areas of convergence in addressing legislative and supervisory developments within the European Union. Cooperation with the FMA also has an important bilateral dimension, given the significant presence of Austrian groups and entities in Romania’s financial market. We will continue to deepen the excellent relationship between the two institutions and support an efficient exchange of information and expertise. In this way, we contribute to promoting high and convergent standards of regulation and supervision, strengthening institutional capacity, and maintaining stable, efficient and resilient financial markets in which participants can have confidence.” Mariana Kühnel’s visit to Bucharest comes at a time when European supervisory authorities are placing increasing emphasis on strengthening the Single Market and aligning regulatory and supervisory practices across Europe. The discussions on the implementation of the IRRD, developments concerning the Markets Integration and Supervision Package, and the challenges associated with crypto-assets highlight the need for close cooperation between national authorities, including through the regular exchange of experience and best practices. At the same time, the relationship between the ASF and the FMA has an important bilateral dimension, given the significant presence of Austrian groups and entities in Romania’s financial market. Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto/Getty Images Spain Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request Timothy Pratt Fri 20 Nov 2026 13.34 EST Last modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 13.36 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza. Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”. US seized American heir’s cellphone in violation of treaty agreement, lawyer says Read more Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.” An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza. The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish. The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations. The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request. The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website . The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”. Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.” The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case. Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland , Ciarán Mulholland. Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.” The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”. “It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added. “This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.
